---
title: Receive webhooks
description: Keep your own records in step with each video's state, from signed webhook events and a catch-up job for any you miss.
---

ClipMux tells your backend when something happens to a video: it's ready,
it failed, its subtitles are done, it was deleted. Each event is an HTTP
POST to a URL of yours, signed with your webhook secret. Your handler finds
the record the video belongs to, by your own `passthrough`, and stores what
changed.

## Before you start

- A webhook endpoint registered for your app, and its secret as
  `CLIPMUX_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. `npx @clipmux/node init` makes both when the
  owner gives a webhook URL on the approval page. Otherwise add one under
  **Apps & API**, your app, **Webhooks** in the dashboard, or with
  `clipmux admin create-webhook --app NAME --url URL` on the server.
- Uploads made with a `passthrough`, your own ID for the record; see
  [Link videos to your records](/docs/build/upload/passthrough).
- While you develop on a laptop the server can't reach, forward events with
  [listen](/docs/build/webhooks/listen).

## The events

| Event | When |
| --- | --- |
| `video.asset.ready` | The video is encoded and plays. |
| `video.asset.updated` | Its title changed. |
| `video.asset.errored` | It failed; `error_code` on the video says why. |
| `video.asset.reencode_failed` | A re-encode failed. The video still plays its previous encode. |
| `video.asset.deleted` | It was deleted. |
| `video.asset.track.ready` | A subtitles or chapters track is ready. |
| `video.asset.track.errored` | A track failed; `track.error_code` says why. |
| `video.asset.track.deleted` | A track was deleted. |

Each body has the event's `id` (`evt_…`), `type`, `created_at` and `data`,
the video as `GET /v1/assets/{id}` returned it when the event was made.
Track events add `track: {id, kind, error_code?}`, and re-encode events add
`job`. Every field is in [Webhook events](/docs/reference/webhooks).

## Handle them with clipmuxHandler [#handle-them-with-clipmuxhandler]

`clipmuxHandler` from `@clipmux/node/handlers` verifies each request, then
re-fetches the video, so your code sees its current state rather than the
state when the event was made:

```ts title="app/api/clipmux/[action]/route.ts"
import { clipmuxHandler } from '@clipmux/node/handlers'

export const POST = clipmuxHandler({
  // Every verified event, before asset(). Optional.
  async event(event) {
    console.log(event.type, event.id)
  },
  // The video, re-fetched so it's current, and the event that triggered it.
  async asset(asset, event) {
    await db.lesson.update({
      where: { ref: asset.passthrough },
      data: { status: asset.status, playbackId: asset.playback_ids[0]?.id },
    })
  },
  // Errors the handler turned into a 4xx or 5xx. Default: console.error for 5xx.
  onError(err, req) {
    logger.warn({ err }, 'clipmux handler')
  },
})
```

The webhook route is `/api/clipmux/webhook` on your app. ClipMux POSTs to
the URL you registered, so register that one. What the handler does with each
request:

1. Verifies the signature and timestamp. A request that fails gets `400`
   with the reason (`missing_header`, `stale`, `bad_signature` or
   `invalid_body`), and your callbacks aren't called.
2. Calls `event(event)`, if you passed it.
3. Calls `asset(asset, event)` with the video from `GET /v1/assets/{id}`.
   If the video is gone (`404`), it passes the event's copy instead. Within
   one process, it skips a video whose `version` is older than one it has
   already passed you.
4. Answers `200 {"received": true}`.

If `event` or `asset` throws, the handler answers with a `5xx` and ClipMux retries
the delivery, for up to 24 hours. Throw when your own database fails;
return normally for anything you mean to ignore.

`event` narrows on `type`, so a track event has its `track`:

```ts
async event(event) {
  if (event.type === 'video.asset.track.ready') console.log(event.track.kind) // 'subtitles' | 'chapters'
},
```

## Write the handler to be safe [#write-the-handler-to-be-safe]

Delivery is **at least once** and **unordered**. The same event can arrive
twice, and `video.asset.ready` can arrive after a later
`video.asset.updated`. Write your handler so that doesn't matter:

- **Upsert by `passthrough`.** Find your record by `asset.passthrough` and
  set its fields, rather than appending or counting.
- **Keep the highest `version`.** Every change to a video raises its
  `version`. Store the one you applied and skip any video with a lower one.
  The handler does this within one process, but not across restarts or
  several instances of your app.
- **Dedupe on the event ID** if an event triggers something that mustn't
  run twice, such as an email. `event.id` is the same as the `X-Webhook-Id`
  header, and stays the same on every retry.
- **Ignore what isn't yours.** Answer `200` for an event whose
  `passthrough` you don't know, so ClipMux doesn't retry it.

A video's status on your record:

| Video `status` | Your record |
| --- | --- |
| `waiting_upload` | Uploading |
| `processing` | Processing |
| `ready`, with an active playback ID | Ready |
| `errored` or `deleted` | Failed or removed |

Tracks are made after the video is ready, so `video.asset.ready` is
written first, then `video.asset.track.ready` or `video.asset.track.errored`.
Delivery is unordered, though: events written a moment apart can arrive the
other way round. Keep the highest `data.version` you've seen, or re-fetch
the asset.

## Catch up on missed events [#catch-up-on-missed-events]

If your endpoint is down for longer than the 24 hours of retries, its
events are dropped. Run a catch-up job, for example every few minutes or at
start, that walks every video changed since the last run:

```ts
let since = await db.state.get('clipmux_since') // a Date or ISO string you stored
const startedAt = new Date()
for await (const asset of clipmux.assets.changes({ since })) {
  await applyAsset(asset) // the same upsert as your asset callback
}
await db.state.set('clipmux_since', startedAt)
```

`assets.changes` pages through `GET /v1/assets?updated_since=…`, oldest
first, deleted videos included. Because your upsert keeps the highest
`version`, running it alongside webhooks is safe.

## Verify by hand

Without `clipmuxHandler`, verify each request yourself with the raw body:

```ts
import { ClipMux, WebhookVerificationError } from '@clipmux/node'

const clipmux = new ClipMux()

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const raw = await req.text() // the exact bytes; never parse and re-serialize
  let event
  try {
    event = await clipmux.webhooks.verify(raw, req.headers)
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof WebhookVerificationError) return new Response(null, { status: 400 })
    throw err
  }
  const asset = await clipmux.assets.get(event.data.id) // the body says something changed; re-fetch what
  await applyAsset(asset)
  return new Response(null, { status: 200 })
}
```

Any `2xx` counts as delivered. Redirects aren't followed. For the scheme
and Python, Go and PHP, see
[Verify webhook signatures](/docs/build/webhooks/verify-signatures).

## Check it works

With your app running, upload a short file and watch the events arrive:

```bash
npx @clipmux/node upload sample.mp4 --passthrough lesson_42 --wait
```

Your `asset` callback runs for `video.asset.ready` and your record shows the
video as ready. If nothing arrives, open **Deliveries** on the endpoint in
the dashboard: each try shows its HTTP status or error.

- `400` with `bad_signature`: the secret is wrong, or a middleware parsed
  the body before the handler read it.
- `400` with `stale`: your server's clock is more than 5 minutes off.
- `404`: the URL isn't the handler's `/webhook` route, or you passed
  neither `asset` nor `event`.
- `connection_failed` or `timeout`: ClipMux can't reach the URL, or your
  handler took longer than 10 seconds.
